Reserved on 28.09.2026
Delivered on 14.10.2026
HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Reference No. 01 of 2026
In the Matter of Capital Punishment
Awarded to Sanjay Singh --Appellant

Versus
State of Uttarakhand
--Respondent
Presence:-
Mr. Arvind Vashistha, Amicus Curiae assisted by Mr. Prateek Tripathi and

Ms. Neelima Mishra Joshi, Amicus Curiae for the appellant.

Coram: Hon'ble Ravindra Maithani, J.
Hon'ble Siddhartha Sah, J.
Hon'ble Ravindra Maithani, J.
In Sessions Trial No. 02 of 2015, State v. Sanjay Singh
("the sessions trial"), by the impugned judgment and order dated
21.02.2026/24.02.2026, passed by Additional Sessions Judge,
Tehri Garhwal, the appellant Sanjay has been convicted under
Sections 302, 316 and 201 IPC and sentenced as under:-
1

UKHC010036772026
(i) Under Section 302 IPC - Death sentence
with a fine of Rs. 10,000/- and in default
of payment of fine, to undergo further
imprisonment for a period of six months.
(ii) Under Section 316 IPC - Rigorous
imprisonment for a period of three years
with a fine of Rs. 5,000/- and in default of
payment of fine, to undergo further
imprisonment for a period of six months.
(iii) Under Section 201 IPC - Rigorous
imprisonment for a period of two years
with a fine of Rs. 5,000/- and in default of
payment, to undergo further imprisonment
for a period of six months.
2. Criminal Reference No. 01 of 2026 has been instituted
under Section 366 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 ("the
Code") for confirmation of death sentence as awarded to the
appellant Sanjay Singh.
3. Criminal Appeal No. 224 of 2026 has been preferred by
the appellant Sanjay Singh against his conviction and sentence, as
stated hereinabove.
4. Facts necessary to appreciate the controversy, briefly
stated are as follows. One Ram Singh Panwar of village Gumalgaon
lodged a report on 13.12.2024 to the concerned Revenue Officer
that his son/appellant Sanjay Singh has killed his real brother
Surendra Singh, his mother Smt. Meena Devi and his sister-in-law
2

UKHC010036772026
Smt. Kanta Devi by a sword. This report is Ex. A2. Based on it, at
Revenue Police Circle Kwili, Tehsil Gaja, Block Narendra Nagar,
District Tehri Garhwal, chik FIR, Ex. A6 was lodged and case
registered.
5. For the purposes of the instant matter, the facts need
not be gone into details. Sufficient to state that after investigation,
charge sheet, Ex. A 33, was submitted against the appellant under
Sections 302, 316, 201 IPC, which is the basis of the sessions trial.
Initially, on 02.05.2015, charges were framed against the appellant
under Sections 302, 316 and 201 IPC, to which he denied and
claimed trial.
6. In order to prove its case, the prosecution initially
examined 16 witnesses, namely, PW 1 Lal Singh, PW 2 Gyan
Singh, PW 3 Hans Lal, PW 4 Manik Singh, PW 5 Rajendra Singh,
PW 6 Bhagwan Singh Panwar, PW 7 Smt. Shashi Devi, PW 8 Gulab
Singh, PW 9 Ramesh Nautiyal, PW 10 Jai Singh Chauhan, PW 11
Dr. Anil Kumar Singh, PW 12 Gambhir Singh, PW 13 Dr. Vinay
Sharma, PW 14 Dr. Mahesh Kumar Khetan, PW 15 Dr. Ravi Gupta
and PW 16 Dr. Sudhir Chandra Godiyal.
7. The appellant was examined under Section 313 of the
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 ("the Code"). He denied the
prosecution case. According to him, the investigation was wrong.
8. After hearing the parties, once by the judgment and
order dated 21.08.2021/24.08.2021, the appellant was convicted
under Sections 302, 316 & 201 IPC and sentenced as follows:-
3

UKHC010036772026
(i) Under Section 302 IPC - Death sentence
with a fine of Rs. 5,000/- and in default of
payment of fine, to undergo further
imprisonment for a period of six months.
(ii) Under Section 316 IPC - Rigorous
imprisonment for a period of three years
with a fine of Rs. 2,000/- and in default of
payment of fine, to undergo further
imprisonment for a period of six months.
(iii) Under Section 201 IPC - Rigorous
imprisonment for a period of two years
with a fine of Rs. 2,000/- and in default of
payment, to undergo further imprisonment
for a period of six months.
9. Against this judgment and order dated
21.08.2021/24.08.2021, the appellant preferred Criminal Appeal
No. 441 of 2021, Sanjay Singh v. State of Uttarakhand ("first
appeal"), and for confirmation of death penalty, Reference No. 02 of
2021, in the matter of Capital Punishment awarded to Sanjay
Singh v. State of Uttarakhand ("first reference") was registered,
which were decided on 10.05.2022.
10. In the first reference and the first appeal, the issue
with regard to compliance of Section 329 of the Code and Section
105 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 ("the 2017 Act") was raised
and it was argued that in the instant case, despite there being
record available with regard to mental illness, the Trial Court has
not followed the procedure under Section 329 of the Code. In para
4

UKHC010036772026
11 of the judgment dated 10.05.2022, the Court observed as
follows:-
"11. In this case, apparently the learned Additional Sessions
Judge neither has followed the provisions of Section 329 of the
Code, nor made any resort to Section 105 of the Mental
Healthcare Act. This aspect is not disputed by any of the learned
counsel appearing in this case."
11. This Court in its judgment dated 10.05.2022 passed in
the first reference and the first appeal, referred to various
documents with regard to mental illness of the appellant and
observed that since the appellant was suffering from mental illness
at the time of trial and the steps under Section 329 of the Code
and Section 105 of the 2017 Act were not made applicable, the
trial vitiates. In para 17, the Court observed as follows:-
"17. Thus, it is apparent from the record that there is enough
material on record to be satisfied, prima facie, that the appellant
was suffering from mental illness at the time of trial. In that fact
situation, the operation of Section 329 of the Code as well as
Section 105 of the Mental Healthcare Act come into play. In such
a situation, the Court should have followed the procedure laid
down under Section 329 of the Code read with Section 105 of the
Mental Healthcare Act. As the learned Trial Judge has not
followed the procedure prescribed, the entire trial is vitiated, and
hence, the appeal has to be allowed."
12. Accordingly, the first appeal was allowed and the
matter was remanded. In paras 19 and 20, the Hon'ble Court
observed as follows:-
"19. In that view of the matter, we are of the opinion that the
matter should be reconsidered by the learned trial judge from the
stage when it was first brought to her notice that the appellant is
suffering from mental illness.
20. In the result, the appeal is allowed. The judgment of
conviction and death sentence are hereby set aside. The death
reference is answered accordingly. The matter is remanded back
to the court of learned Additional Sessions Judge, Tehri Garhwal
to re-hear the matter by following the observations made by us in
5

UKHC010036772026
the preceding paragraphs of this judgment."
13. After the sessions trial was received from remand, on
22.06.2022, the trial court observed that the appellant is required
to be examined by Psychiatrist or Psychologist. Accordingly, the
court made a communication to the Chief Medical Superintendent,
State Mental Health Institute, Selaqui, Dehradun ("the Institute").
Reports were received that the appellant is a patient of "Psychosis
NOS" and not fit for trial. The Medical Board also opined that it
could not be said as to what was the mental condition of the
appellant on 13.12.2014, on which date the offence was
committed. This was mentioned in court's order dated 15.11.2022
and further report was sought. Another report dated 21.11.2022
was received from the Institute, which records as under:-
"Sh. Sanjay Singh S/o- Sh. Ram Singh is presently
admitted in State Mental Health Institute, Selaqui Dehradun from
23-07-2022. He was referred to department of Clinical
Psychology, NIEPVD Rajpur road Dehradun (NIVH) for
Psychological assessment (reports attached). He was examined by
the board at State Mental Health Institute, Selaqui Dehradun on
dt. 26-09-2022 for his current mental status which has been
opined as follows-1- Based on available history and detailed evaluation Sh.
Sanjay Singh S/o Sh. Ram Singh has been
provisionally diagnosed as a case of Psychosis NOS.
2- Patient is not fit for trial because of his ongoing illness.
He is not having Capacity. Rogi vartman me chal rahi
paristhitiyon, ghatnakram evam unke sambhawit
parinaamon ko thik se samajhne me asmarth hai.
3- His mental status on date 13/12/2014 cannot be
commented upon, only present mental status can be
commented upon.
4- Patient can be referred to higher centre for second
opinion for confirmatory diagnosis. (AIIMS Rishikesh,
AIIMS Delhi, IHBAS)"
14. This finds mention in the court's order dated
6

UKHC010036772026
29.11.2022. Thereafter, another report dated 13.12.2022 of the
Institute was received (Ex. A-40), which records the conditions of
the appellant as below:-
"Shri Sanjay Singh S/o Shri Ram Singh has been admitted
in State Mental Health Institute, Selaqui Dehradun on 23-07-
2022 and examined by the board at SMHI, Selaqui Dehradun on
12.12.2022 for her (sic his) current mental status for has opined
as follows:-
Based on available history, examination and detailed
evaluation done by clinical Psychologist (Reports attached) Shri
Sanjay Singh has been provisionally diagnosed as a case of
Psychosis NOS (Psychosis Not otherwise Specified).
Patient is fit for trial.
His Mental Status on date 13-12-2014 cannot be
commented upon, only present Mental Status can be commented
upon.
Patient can be referred to higher centre for second opinion
for confirmatory diagnosis (AIIMS Rishikesh, AIIMS Delhi,
IHBAS)."
15. The court took note of this report dated 13.12.2022 in
its order dated 01.02.2023. Finally, taking note of all these
developments, the trial court on 23.02.2022 observed that since
report is received that the appellant is fit for trial, the trial shall
proceed. Thereafter, the sequence of events is as follows:-
(i) 03.04.2023 - Charges under Sections 302,
316, 201 IPC were framed against the appellant,
to which he denied and claimed trial.
(ii) 24.05.2023 - On behalf of the District
Government Counsel (Criminal), it was informed
to the court that the witnesses who have been
examined earlier, their examination-in-chief may
be read into evidence. This was noted and
witnesses were called for cross-examination. On
7

UKHC010036772026
that date, PW 1 Lal Singh and PW 3 Hans Lal
were cross-examined.
(iii) 02.04.2024 - Prosecution evidence was
closed and the matter was listed for examination
of the appellant under Section 313 of the Code.
(iv) 25.04.2024 - The court observed that the
appellant is not answering to any question under
Section 313 of the Code, therefore, he may be
examined by All India Institute of Medical
Sciences, Rishikesh ("AIIMS, Rishikesh").
(v) 24.05.2024 - The Medical Board of AIIMS,
Rishikesh gave a report that a Board has been
constituted and the appellant requires
admission and treatment at AIIMS, Rishikesh.
(vi) 25.05.2024 - The court took note of the
report of the Medical Board of AIIMS, Rishikesh
dated 24.05.2024.
(vii) 07.06.2024- The Medical Board of AIIMS,
Rishikesh gave its report dated 07.06.2024. It
records as follows:-
"(i) The patient is suffering from
Schizophrenia - currently in partial
remission. After starting Tablet
Risperidone 8 mg/d in divided doses.
(ii) The patient requires continued
treatment and regular follow-ups.
(iii) At present, the patient appears fit to
stand trial."
(viii) 10.07.2024- The court took note of the
8

UKHC010036772026
report dated 07.06.2024 of AIIMS, Rishikesh,
but did not pass any order on it. The court
simply made a mention of it and recorded that
the appellant is not answering to any question
asked under Section 313 of the Code.
(ix) 29.07.2024- The appellant was questioned
under Section 313 of the Code, but he did not
give any answer.
(x) 24.10.2024- Again the appellant was
questioned under Section 313 of the Code, but
he did not give any answer.
(xi) 11.12.2024- Again on this date, the
appellant was questioned under Section 313 of
the Code, but he did not answer any question.
The court made an inference that it seems the
appellant has nothing to say and got the
signature of the appellant on the statement
under Section 313 of the Code and thereafter by
the impugned judgment, convicted and
sentenced the appellant, which gives rise to the
appeal as well as to the reference.
16. Learned Amicus Curiae submits that a Coordinate
Bench of this Court in its judgment dated 10.05.2022 passed in
the first reference and the first appeal had taken note of various
certificates of the appellants, namely, Exs. A 34, A 36, A 38, A 39
in paragraphs 13, 14 & 15 and concluded in paragraph 17 of the
judgment that since the procedures under Section 329 of the Code
and 105 of the 2017 Act have not been followed, the entire trial is
9

UKHC010036772026
vitiated and, therefore, directed the court below to reconsider the
matter from the stage when it was first brought to the notice that
the appellant is suffering from mental illness. It is argued that
thereafter though the trial court had framed charges on
03.04.2023 afresh, but did not follow the due procedure. It is
argued that whatever evidence was recorded earlier, that has been
vitiated due to non-compliance of Section 329 of the Code and
Section 105 of the 2017 Act. Moreover, it is argued that a witness
is to be examined in the presence of an accused under Section 273
of the Code, but if the appellant was mentally unwell, his physical
presence makes no difference and it will be presumed that, in fact,
the evidence that was recorded earlier was not recorded in the
presence of the appellant.
17. It is argued that on 24.05.2023, the court noted on the
endorsement of the prosecution that the witnesses, that were
examined earlier, their examination-in-chief may be read into
evidence. It is argued that this examination-in-chief of the
witnesses recorded earlier has already been vitiated by the
judgment dated 10.05.2022 passed by this Court in the first
appeal and the reference, and the court below committed an error
in treating that evidence as examination-in-chief. It is argued that,
in fact, it is no evidence against the appellant, except evidence of
PW 17 Dr. Ravindra Navani, who was examined afresh and the
prosecution, accordingly, has utterly failed to prove the charges
against the appellant; he deserves to be acquitted. It is argued that
there are still reports that the appellant is mentally ill, this Court
needs to pass an order under Sections 334, 335 of the Code and
under Section 103 of the 2017 Act so that the appellant may be
10

UKHC010036772026
sent in a facility for his treatment.
18. In addition to it, it is argued that, in fact, in the instant
case, even after remand of the case by order dated 10.05.2022
passed in the first appeal and the first reference, the compliance
under Section 329 of the Code has not been made. The appellant
did not reply to any question under Section 313 of the Code. He
was suffering with Schizophrenia. The trial ought to have been
suspended. It is argued that for this reason also, the trial has been
vitiated and the appellant now deserves to be acquitted of the
charges levelled against him.
19. Learned Senior Counsel Mr. Arvind Vashistha further
argued that the record, which is available proves in abundance
that, in fact, the appellant was mentally ill on the date of incident
itself, because soon after the incident on 14.12.2014, when he was
produced before the Magistrate, before that he was examined by
the doctor, who opined that the appellant was suffering with
mental illness. It is argued that the record shows that at the time
of incident, the appellant was unaware of the act committed by
him and its consequences, therefore also, he deserves acquittal.
20. In support of his contention, learned Senior Counsel
has placed reliance on the principle of law as laid down in the case
of Accused 'X' v. State of Maharashtra, (2019) 7 SCC 1, wherein in
paras 70 and 71, the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed as follows:-
"70. In line with the above discussion, we note that there appear
to be no set disorders/disabilities for evaluating the "severe
mental illness", however a "test of severity" can be a guiding factor
for recognising those mental illness which qualify for an
exemption. Therefore, the test envisaged herein predicates that
11

UKHC010036772026
the offender needs to have a severe mental illness or disability,
which simply means that a medical professional would objectively
consider the illness to be most serious so that he cannot
understand or comprehend the nature and purpose behind the
imposition of such punishment. These disorders generally include
schizophrenia, other serious psychotic disorders and dissociative
disorders with schizophrenia.
71. The following directions need to be followed in the future
cases in light of the above discussion:
71.1. That the post-conviction severe mental illness will be a
mitigating factor that the appellate court, in appropriate cases,
needs to consider while sentencing an accused to death penalty.
71.2. The assessment of such disability should be conducted by a
multi-disciplinary team of qualified professionals (experienced
medical practitioners, criminologists, etc.), including professional
with expertise in accused's particular mental illness.
71.3. The burden is on the accused to prove by a preponderance
of clear evidence that he is suffering with severe mental illness.
The accused has to demonstrate active, residual or prodromal
symptoms, that the severe mental disability was manifesting.
71.4. The State may offer evidence to rebut such claim.
71.5. Court in appropriate cases could set up a panel to submit
an expert report.
71.6. "Test of severity" envisaged herein predicates that the
offender needs to have a severe mental illness or disability, which
simply means that objectively the illness needs to be most serious
that the accused cannot understand or comprehend the nature
and purpose behind the imposition of such punishment."
21. Learned Senior Counsel also submits that now the
case need not be remanded. The appellant is already in custody for
more than 11 years. He is entitled to benefit of Section 84 of IPC.
Hence, it is a case of acquittal.
22. Ms. Neelima Mishra Joshi, learned counsel for the
appellant Sanjay submits that the appellant was suffering with
mental illness and the trial court has not considered this aspect
and even the statement of the complainant has not been recorded.
23. Learned Senior Counsel Mr. J.S. Virk appearing for the
12

UKHC010036772026
State submits that, in fact, from day one the appellant was
suffering with mental illness. He would submit that subsequently
on 20.03.2023, after remand of the case, the court has recorded
that the appellant is able to defend himself and he is fit for trial,
which means that compliance of Section 329 of the Code has been
made. Learned Senior Counsel also raised the following points in
his submission:-
(i) On 24.05.2023, on behalf of the prosecution, it
was stated that the examination-in-chief of the
witnesses recorded earlier may be treated as
examination-in-chief and accordingly, the
witnesses were further cross-examined by the
appellant. It is argued that at that stage, the
appellant did not raise any objection, hence, the
examination is valid.
(ii) If the appellant was not answering to questions
under Section 313 of the Code, the court below
ought to have further examined the appellant by
a mental health care professional or by a doctor.
It was not done, which is against the spirit of
Section 329 of the Code and for this reason, the
matter may be remanded.
(iii) On the issue of application of Section 84 IPC, it
is argued that from day one, the appellant was
mentally ill, but he only harmed his family
members and concealed his presence. Therefore,
it is argued that the appellant was aware of his
acts.
13

UKHC010036772026
24. First and foremost, this Court will examine as to
whether the compliance of Section 329 of the Code has been made
or not?
25. In its judgment dated 10.05.2022, the Coordinate
Bench of this Court, in the first reference and the first appeal, has
observed in para 11 that the trial court has not followed the
provisions of Section 329 of the Code and Section 105 of the 2017
Act. This statement is not completely correct. In fact, the complete
fact was not brought before the Court when the first reference and
the first appeal were decided. It will be a little detailed but
necessary to reproduce as to what had happened in this matter.
26. The following dates would be necessary to be noted:-
(i) 13.12.2024 - The date of incident.
(ii) 14.12.2024- The Investigating Officer gave
an application to the Medical Officer, District
Hospital, Baurari, New Tehri for medical
examination of the appellant.
(iii) 14.12.2014- The appellant was examined
by the Medical Officer at District Hospital,
Baurari, New Tehri (Ex. A-36) and the doctor
opined that "this person is physically fit but
mentally illness may be present so referred to
clinical Psychologist for evaluation of his
illness." Despite this medical report, the
appellant was remanded to judicial custody on
14.12.2014.
(iv) 09.01.2015- Incharge Jailor, District Jail,
14

UKHC010036772026
New Tehri, District Tehri Garhwal sought
permission from the court that the appellant has
been referred to the Institute by the Incharge
Medical Officer, Jail, therefore, permission may
be granted to shift the appellant to the Institute.
(v) 02.05.2015- Charges were framed against
the appellant.
(vi) 02.06.2015- PW 1 Lal Singh and PW 2
Gyan Singh were examined.
(vii) 21.07.2015- Examination of PW 3 Hans
Lal, PW 4 Manik Singh and PW 5 Rajendra
Singh.
(viii) 31.07.2015- Letter by Incharge Jailor,
District Jail, New Tehri to the court seeking
permission to send the appellant to the Institute
on the ground that he was to be admitted in the
institute as per the medical advice.
(ix) 13.08.2015- Examination of PW 6 Bhagwan
Singh Panwar.
(x) 21.08.2015- Letter of Chief Medical
Superintendent of the Institute addressed to the
Superintendent, District Jail, Tehri Garhwal
seeking permission that the appellant is to be
referred to higher institute.
(xi) 26.08.2015- The communication of
Incharge Jailor, District Jail, New Tehri to the
court. On this, the court did not forward the
appellant to the higher institute on the ground
that there is no report placed along with it.
15

UKHC010036772026
(xii) 07.09.2015- Examination of PW 7 Smt.
Shashi Devi and PW 8 Gulab Singh.
(xiii) 17.09.2015- Examination of PW 9 Ramesh
Nautiyal and PW 10 Jai Singh Chauhan.
(xiv) 21.09.2015- Communication of Incharge
Jailor, District Jail, New Tehri seeking
permission to refer the appellant to the higher
institute.
(xv) 05.11.2015- Examination of PW 11 Dr. Anil
Kumar Singh.
(xvi) 13.11.2015- Communication of Incharge
Jailor, District Jail, New Tehri seeking
permission of the court to shift the appellant to
higher institute. It records that the condition of
the appellant is aggressive. All the other inmates
are scared of him. He may commit any untoward
incident. On it, the court directed that the Jail
Superintendent may take steps in accordance
with the Jail Manual.
(xvii) 20.11.2015- Examination of PW 12
Gambhir Singh.
(xviii) 22.01.2016- On this date, the court
proceeded to record the statement of the
appellant under Section 313 of the Code, but the
appellant was not answering about his name,
his father's name, the name of his village, etc.
Thereafter, the medical reports of the appellant
were sought from jail and from this stage, the
trial deferred. It is, in fact, a step under Section
16

UKHC010036772026
329 of the Code.
(xix) 12.02.2021- Finally, the court observed
that the appellant told the court that he is fit to
stand trial. The court sought report and on
31.03.2021, based on the medical report, which
recorded that the appellant is fit to stand trial,
the court recorded that the trial shall resume.
(xx) The above events make it abundantly clear that
the trial remained suspended from 22.01.2016
till 31.03.2021. This is a fact. But, fact also
remains that in this period, the appellant was
mentally unwell.
27. There are a few more reports, which need mention at
this stage only.
(i) 11.02.2016- The appellant was examined
by the Government Medical College, Haldwani
(Ex. A-39) and the doctor recorded as below:-
"Accused Mr. Sanjay Singh (Age-30y/M,
PANA No. 247495) S/o Shri Ram Singh was
admitted here, on 01-02-2016 for observation,
opinion & treatment. During his hospitalization, we
could not observe any behaviour abnormality
suggestive of any psychiatric/psychotic
(unsoundness of mind) disorder, except mutism
(aphonia) which is more likely to be malingering in
present situation of the case.
Since, we could not yet reach any diagnostic
conclusion, therefore, initiation of treatment was
not feasible. To reach at an appropriate diagnosis,
we shall need his behavior history before his arrest
from his closed relative/neighbors and thereafter,
he may be appropriately managed."
(ii) 11.08.2016- The appellant was examined at
17

UKHC010036772026
the Institute (Ex. A-34) and the doctor opined
that "Did not suggestive of clear major
psychotic disorder. However, for definite
opinion psychological assessment at higher
centre may be done by clinical psychologist".
(iii) 23.09.2019- The Board of AIIMS, Rishikesh
examined (Ex. A-38) the appellant and observed
as follows:-
(i) Mr. Sanjay Singh s/o Sh. Ram Singh has
been diagnosed as a case of Schizophrenia
and is improving with the given treatment.
(ii) At present he is not totally asymptomatic
but a significant improvement has been
observed with the treatment.
(iii) Based on present observation, at present he
is able to manage his activities of daily living
independently.
(iv) Patient requires long term treatment and

(iv) 06.04.2021- The appellant was examined
under Section 313 of the Code.
(v) 07.07.2021- After resumption of trial, on
07.07.2021, the court observed that the
witnesses with regard to treatment of the mental
illness of the appellant need to be examined.
(vi) 26.07.2021- PW 13 Dr. Vinay Sharma and
PW 14 Dr. Mahesh Kumar Khetan were
examined.
(vii) 31.07.2021- PW 15 Dr. Ravi Gupta was
examined.
(viii) 02.08.2021- PW 16 Dr. Sudhir Chandra
Godiyal was examined.
(ix) 04.08.2021- Additional statement of the
18

UKHC010036772026
appellant under Section 313 of the Code was
recorded.
(x) 24.08.2021- The court below convicted and
sentenced the appellants under Sections 302,
316 and 201 IPC.
28. Section 329 of the Code reads as under:-
"329. Procedure in case of person of unsound
mind tried before Court.-(1) If at the trial of any person
before a Magistrate or Court of Session, it appears to the
Magistrate or Court that such person is of unsound mind
and consequently incapable of making his defence, the
Magistrate or Court shall, in the first instance, try the fact
of such unsoundness and incapacity, and if the Magistrate
or Court, after considering such medical and other
evidence as may be produced before him or it, is satisfied
of the fact, he or it shall record a finding to that effect and
shall postpone further proceedings in the case.
(1A) If during trial, the Magistrate or Court of
Sessions finds the accused to be of unsound mind, he or it
shall refer such person to a psychiatrist or clinical
psychologist for care and treatment, and the psychiatrist
or clinical psychologist, as the case may be shall report to
the Magistrate or Court whether the accused is suffering
from unsoundness of mind:
Provided that if the accused is aggrieved by the
information given by the psychiatric or clinical
psychologist, as the case may be, to the Magistrate, he
may prefer an appeal before the Medical Board which shall
consist of-
(a) head of psychiatry unit in the nearest
government hospital; and
(b) a faculty member in psychiatry in the nearest
medical college.
(2) If such Magistrate or Court is informed that the
person referred to in sub-section (1A) is a person of
unsound mind, the Magistrate or Court shall further
determine whether unsoundness of mind renders the
accused incapable of entering defence and if the accused is
found so incapable, the Magistrate or Court shall record a
finding to that effect and shall examine the record of
evidence produced by the prosecution and after hearing
19

UKHC010036772026
the advocate of the accused but without questioning the
accused, if the Magistrate or Court finds that no prima
facie case is made out against the accused, he or it shall,
instead of postponing the trial, discharge the accused and
deal with him in the manner provided under section 330:
Provided that if the Magistrate or Court finds that a
prima facie case is made out against the accused in
respect of whom a finding of unsoundness of mind is
arrived at, he shall postpone the trial for such period, as in
the opinion of the psychiatrist or clinical psychologist, is
required for the treatment of the accused.
(3) If the Magistrate or Court finds that a prima
facie case is made out against the accused and he is
incapable of entering defence by reason of mental
retardation, he or it shall not hold the trial and order the
accused to be dealt with in accordance with section 330."
29. In fact, the laudable object behind Section 329 of the
Code is to help a person, who is of unsound mind. That moment,
the litigation no more remains adversarial. After all, if a person is
not able to understand the proceeding before him, there is no
question of going ahead with the proceedings, because such an
accused may not be in a position to defend himself. He may not be
in a position to tell his defence counsel as to how to proceed
ahead.
30. In the case of Prakash Nayi alias Sen v. State of Goa,
(2023) 5 SCC 673, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as follows:-
"15. Chapter XXV of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
(hereinafter "CrPC"), though procedural in nature, also becomes
substantive when it deals with an accused person of unsound
mind. A well-laid procedure is contemplated under Sections 328
to 339CrPC. There is not even a need for an application under
Section 329CrPC in finding out as to whether an accused would
be sound enough to stand a trial, rather it is the mandatory duty
of the court. Under Section 330, the court can even go to the
extent of discharging such a person if his inability to stand trial
continues with a rigid chance of improvement. As per Section
334CrPC, the judgment of the court shall include a specific
20

UKHC010036772026
finding that the act was committed due to unsoundness of mind,
though it was actually done. The reason is simple as there cannot
be an acquittal on the ground of unsoundness of mind unless the
act is actually done.
16. The whole idea under the provisions discussed is to facilitate
a person of unsound mind to stand trial, not only because of his
reasoning capacity, but also to treat him as the one who is having
a disability. The role of the court is to find the remedial measures
and do complete justice.
17. Having noted the scope and ambit of Chapter XXV CrPC,
including the provisions incorporated by way of amendments in
the year 2009, one has to take into account the fact that the court
has a larger role to play while considering the case under Section
84IPC. If a friendly approach is required to be followed during the
trial, when adequate powers have been conferred upon the court
to even discharge an accused on the ground of an unsound mind,
the same reasoning will have to be applied with much force when
it comes to Section 84IPC."
31. The appellant, in the instant case, was found by the
doctors suffering with mental illness on 14.12.2014 before he was
produced before the Magistrate. This was the first stage.
Thereafter, there had been multiple communications during trial
with regard to the mental health condition of the appellant.
Particularly, Exs. A 34, A 36, A 38 and A 39, which have been
referred to hereinbefore, make it abundantly clear that the
appellant was suffering with Schizophrenia. But, his trial
continued and statements of PW 1 to PW 12 were recorded during
that period. That trial was held vitiated by this Court by its
judgment dated 10.05.2022 passed in the first reference and the
first appeal.
32. Subsequently, when the trial resumed after remand of
the case, on 24.05.2023, the examination-in-chief recorded
between 02.06.2015 to 19.01.2016 were also considered for
examination-in-chief. Section 273 of the Code is also important. It
21

UKHC010036772026
records that the evidence is to be taken in presence of the accused.
It reads as follows:-
"273. Evidence to be taken in presence of accused.-
Except as otherwise expressly provided, all evidence taken in the
course of the trial or other proceeding shall be taken in the
presence of the accused, or, when his personal attendance is
dispensed with, in the presence of his pleader:
Provided that where the evidence of a woman below the
age of eighteen years who is alleged to have been subjected to
rape or any other sexual offence, is to be recorded, the court may
take appropriate measures to ensure that such woman is not
confronted by the accused while at the same time ensuring the
right of cross-examination of the accused.
Explanation.-In this section, "accused" includes a person
in relation to whom any proceeding under Chapter VIII has been
commenced under this Code."
33. Above provision has a reason. An accused needs to
know as to what is being spoken against him and by whom, so that
he may put his defence. From 02.05.2015 to 19.01.2016, the
appellant was mentally unwell. There are multiple reports during
that period, as has been stated hereinbefore. But, the examination-in-chief recorded during that period of PW 1 to PW 12 was further
taken into consideration.
34. When the appellant was mentally unwell, at the initial
stage, the proceedings ought to have been suspended under
Section 329 of the Code, which was not done and the trial
proceeded from 02.06.2015 onwards. It is non-compliance of
Section 329 of the Code.
35. After judgment of this Court passed in the first
reference and the first appeal, on 10.05.2022, the court sought a
report about the mental condition of the appellant and on
22

UKHC010036772026
01.02.2023, relying on the report dated 13.12.2022 of the
Institute, which is Ex. A-40, proved by PW 17 Dr. Ravindra Navani,
proceeded with the trial. This report has already been quoted
hereinabove (at para 14 of the judgment). It records that the
appellant has been provisionally diagnosed as a case of Psychosis
NOS and further that the patient can be referred to higher centre
for second opinion for confirmatory diagnosis (AIIMS Rishikesh,
AIIMS Delhi, IHBAS). What happened thereafter? Again on
20.03.2023, the court believed on the report dated 13.12.2022 of
the Institute (Ex. A-40) and proceeded with the trial and framed
charges, etc. The case remained for cross-examination from
24.05.2023 to 02.04.2024.
36. The first date for examination of the appellant under
Section 313 of the Code was 12.04.2024. He did not answer any
question. Therefore, as stated, on 24.04.2024, the court sought
another report from AIIMS, Rishikesh. AIIMS, Rishikesh
constituted a Board and informed the court that the appellant may
be admitted in the hospital for treatment and subsequently a
report was given by the Board on 07.06.2024. It is already quoted
hereinabove (in Para 15(vii) of the judgment). This report was
placed before the court on 10.07.2024, but the court did not stop
the proceedings. This report categorically records that the patient
is suffering with Schizophrenia- currently in partial remission. It
means that the appellant was not mentally well on 07.06.2024
also. But, his trial proceeded. Thereafter, on the next date i.e.
29.07.2024, the appellant was further questioned under Section
313 of the Code, to which he did not answer. He never answered
any question thereafter and as a formality, on 11.12.2024, the
23

UKHC010036772026
court recorded that since the appellant is not answering to any
question, it means that he has nothing to say, and the signatures
of the appellant were obtained.
37. This is a gross non-compliance of the provisions of
Section 329 of the Code. Despite having a positive report dated
07.06.2024 of AIIMS, Rishikesh that the appellant is suffering with
Schizophrenia- currently in partial remission and he requires
continuous treatment and regular follow-ups, the trial proceeded.
It is against the provisions of Section 329 of the Code. Therefore,
this Court is of the view that, in fact, in the instant case, even after
remand of the matter by this Court by its judgment dated
10.05.2022, the provisions of Section 329 of the Code have not
been followed.
38. The question is - should the matter be remanded?
39. It is stated that the appellant is already in custody for
more than 11 years. He is a death row convict twice. Whether the
case should be remanded or not depends on further analysis,
which would be with regard to application of Section 84 IPC and as
to whether the prosecution has been able to prove its case?
40. Since, this Court has already held that in the instant
case, since inception, the provisions of Section 329 of the Code
were not followed and even after remand of the matter by this
Court by judgment dated 10.05.2022 passed in the first reference
and the first appeal, the provisions of Section 329 of the Code have
not been complied with in letter and spirit, this Court may not
24

UKHC010036772026
delve into the evidence that has been adduced by the prosecution.
41. In its order dated 10.05.2022 passed in the first
reference and the first appeal, this Court has already observed in
para 17 that the entire trial has vitiated, which means the evidence
recorded from 02.06.2015 to 06.04.2021 has been vitiated. But,
when after remand, charges were framed on 03.04.2023, thereafter
on 24.05.2023, the examination-in-chief of the witnesses recorded
earlier were taken as examination-in-chief of witnesses. In fact,
that trial had vitiated pursuant to the judgment dated 10.05.2022
passed by this Court in the first reference and the first appeal.
Moreover, as stated, the appellant was not mentally well since
inception. Whatever evidence was recorded from 02.05.2015 till
19.01.2016, the appellant was not able to understand that
evidence. In fact, it was as good as that the evidence was not
recorded in his presence. In other words, the evidence recorded
was in defiance to Section 273 of the Code. Therefore, in fact, there
has been no evidence, except the evidence of PW 17 Dr. Ravindra
Navani. The examination-in-chief of PW 1 to PW 16 were taken
from that evidence, which trial had vitiated. Therefore, also the
prosecution, in fact, has failed to prove the case against the
appellant. There has been no evidence.
42. The last question that requires answer is - as to
whether the appellant is entitled to the benefit of Section 84 IPC?
43. Section 84 of IPC reads as follows:-
"84. Act of a person of unsound mind.-Nothing
is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of
doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of
25

UKHC010036772026
knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is
either wrong or contrary to law."
44. Section 84 of IPC gives protection to such situation
when an act is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, is
incapable of knowing the nature of the act by reason of
unsoundness of mind.
45. In the instant case, there are multiple records to reveal
that the appellant is suffering from mental illness. The first
document is of 14.12.2014. It is Ex. A-36 on record. After arrest, it
is the first document, when the doctor has said that the appellant
is suffering with mental illness. There are repeated documents,
which have been referred to hereinbefore, which reveal that the
appellant is suffering with Psychosis NOS. He is Schizophrenic
patient.
46. At the time of hearing arguments, this Court on
04.08.2026 required that the appellant be produced before the
Director, AIIMS, Rishikesh so as to examine him. The report has
now been received, which reads as under:-
"1. The patient is suffering from Schizophrenia-currently in significantly improved condition, on
daily medication.
2. The patient requires continued treatment and
regular follow-ups for maintenance of improvement.
3. During his current in-patient stay, the patient was
able to communicate verbally without any apparent
difficulty and without requiring any support, and at
present he is fit to stand trial."
26

UKHC010036772026
47. The appellant is still suffering from Schizophrenia. He
is being cured in between. In the case of Prakash Nayi (supra), the
Hon'ble Supreme Court has discussed the concept of mental
illness of Schizophrenia and held that the mere fact that an
accused subsequently became fit to face trial is sufficient to render
an order of acquittal as it is indicative of prior insanity. In para 27
of the judgment in the case of Prakash Nayi (supra), the Hon'ble
Supreme Court observed as follows:
"27. We may also add that this report merely records the
statements of the doctors who have not been examined
before the Court. Suffice it to say, that the evidence of the
government doctor as DW 1 who withstood cross-examination ought to have been accepted. The mere fact
that the appellant subsequently became fit to face the trial
is sufficient enough to render an order of acquittal as it is
indicative of his prior insanity. We do feel that both the
trial court and the High Court were influenced by the
nature of the act while ignoring the condition of the
appellant and the fact that the burden on the accused is
one of preponderance of probability. We have also been
informed that the appellant has recovered fully and mixed
well with the society."
48. In the instant case, it is not that long after the incident
the appellant was examined. He was examined on the next date i.e.
14.12.2014. There had been reports that the appellant needs
treatment for mental illness. Therefore, this Court is of the view
that, in fact, at the time of committing the offence, the appellant by
reason of unsound mind was incapable of knowing the nature of
the act or that what he is doing is either wrong or contrary to law.
Therefore, the appellant is entitled to get benefit under Section 84
of IPC and deserves acquittal.
49. This Court has already held that the prosecution has
27

UKHC010036772026
not been able to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Not only
this, in the instant matter, there has been no compliance of
Section 329 of the Code and the appellant is entitled to benefit of
Section 84 of IPC and deserves acquittal on this count as well.
Now, the question is as to whether the appellant should
be set free?
50. In compliance of this Court's order dated 04.08.2026,
the appellant was produced before the medical board constituted
by the AIIMS, Rishikesh so as to assess his mental condition, and
the said medical board, on the basis of clinical examination and
investigation of the appellant, vide its report dated 25.08.2026 has
categorically opined that the appellant is still suffering from
"Schizophrenia". Thus, since the appellant is suffering from
Schizophrenia, which led to homicidal tendencies in him, this
Court is of the opinion that it is dangerous to let him at liberty and
accordingly, under the provisions of Section 335 of the Code, the
appellant is liable to be detained in safe custody in State Mental
Health Institute, Selaqui, Dehradun. It is needless to add that the
State Government will take steps to have the appellant treated in
the said Institute until he is cured of his illness. Once cured, the
State Government may accommodate the appellant to such
home/accommodation, as per the provisions of the Uttarakhand
Mental Healthcare (Rights of Persons with Mental Illness) Rules,
2023.
51. Accordingly, the Court concludes as under:-
(i) Criminal Appeal No. 224 of 2026 is allowed.
(ii) The judgment and order dated
21.02.2026/24.02.2026 passed in Sessions Trial
No. 02 of 2015, State v. Sanjay Singh is set
aside.

(iii) The appellant is acquitted of the charges under
Sections 302, 316 and 201 IPC.
(iv) Since the appellant is suffering from
Schizophrenia, which led to homicidal
tendencies in him, we are of the opinion that it is
dangerous to let him at liberty and, accordingly,
under the provisions of Section 335 of the Code,
the appellant is directed to be detained in safe
custody in State Mental Health Institute,
